other_side: NLW's lead is that Google's problem is organisational: the arrangement that lost it the coding-agent wave was never going to win it back, so losing Hassabis from day-to-day and Dean altogether may be the reset that lets a redesigned AI org return to the frontier. Zitron's most recent argument bearing on Google's position says the frontier is not the binding constraint, because the customer is missing. Citing UBS's Stephen Ju, he puts Anthropic and OpenAI at 28% of 2026 Google Cloud revenues and more than 48% of 2027 — and reckons Google will have spent roughly $408.5bn in capital expenditure by 2028 to build an AI business of about $80bn a year, most of it selling Anthropic's compute or reselling Anthropic's models through Vertex. His verdict on the whole arrangement is four words: "AI is not working." On that reading, who runs DeepMind changes very little.
truth_beneath: Both men orbit one variable: whether being at the frontier is what determines Google's AI outcome. They agree on more than the tone allows — that Google has spent astonishing sums, that Gemini lost the coding-agent wave, and that much of Google Cloud's AI growth is Anthropic's compute bill. The empirical question is whether non-lab customers will pay Google directly, and the observable that settles it is Alphabet disclosing Cloud or Vertex revenue net of Anthropic and OpenAI spend, read against where Gemini 4 actually lands. The residue is worldview: whether a company's AI fate is decided by talent and org design or by whether anyone is buying. Whittemore is vindicated if a redesigned org ships a genuinely state-of-the-art model within a year and usage follows; Zitron if Google returns to the frontier and the revenue still does not appear. Both are polemicists with incentives — Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype — and the signal is that both treat Google's present position as a failure. Watch Gemini 4's reception.
